slides.title: LLMs in Asset Management
slides.notes: This presentation examines how large language models (LLMs) can support the day-to-day work of an asset manager. Each topic covers the current workflow, relevant industry examples and a proposed application for the firm. The discussion follows front-, middle- and back-office work, using Company A and a quarterly client update as recurring examples. Cover image: an AI-generated research workspace.

slides.title: Scope of proposed LLM applications

shapes.name: !!scope.result
shapes.source: Build applications around the work people need to complete
shapes.english: Proposed applications address specific employee tasks

slides.notes: The inputs are documents, data, messages and business requests. LLMs interpret questions, read and compare material, organize explanations, and draft text or code. Connected tools perform queries, calculations and other operations. Employees check the results and use them to complete research, trading preparation, client communications, review and development tasks.

shapes.name: !!research.repetition

shapes.english: Repeated searching, extraction and checking take time away from analysis

slides.notes: The analyst needs to explain why Company A’s revenue grew and whether that growth can continue. The preparation involves locating comparable revenue and volume data, reading the explanation in meeting notes and comparing two research reports. In this illustrative scenario, prior-quarter and current-quarter revenue are RMB 100m and RMB 110m, while sales volume is 1.0m and 1.1m units. Repeated searches, extraction, calculations and rereading are the work required before the analyst can assess the business. The next three slides show industry approaches to earnings analysis, research synthesis and template preparation.

shapes.source: The LLM links operating evidence to the numbers. Analysts assess the quality of growth.

slides.notes:
Tianhong’s FinAgent breaks a net-profit question into revenue, cost of sales and expenses, then explores drivers such as volume, selling price, raw materials and distribution. The LLM organizes the questions and calls data and calculation tools. Those tools return the figures and calculations. The model connects them to operating and industry information, while the analyst assesses the quality and persistence of growth. Tianhong reported that the time required for manual data preparation and calculations fell from days to minutes.

slides.notes: A request for quote (RFQ) asks counterparties for offer prices and available size. The task is to prepare candidate bonds, current holdings and offer quotes for a potential purchase of Company A bonds maturing within two years. The portfolio manager sets the request. The trader queries market and holdings systems and records the data timestamp, then contacts counterparties with the bond names and buying interest, asks for price and available size, and receives quotes. The trader brings the information together for discussion with the portfolio manager. Systems supply data and counterparties supply quotes. Repeated filters, system switching and copying messages are the preparation steps the proposed application can improve.

slides.notes:
The portfolio manager wants to buy Company A bonds maturing within two years, check current holdings and collect offer quotes. The LLM extracts the issuer, maturity condition and requested data, then calls the business query. Systems return the candidates, maturities and holdings. The trader first requests quotes from counterparties, then provides the received quote messages or quote records. The LLM extracts the bond, clean price and available face value from the supplied records, then combines these details with the system results. In the example, the Company A bond has 1.2 years to maturity, the current holding is RMB 20m face value, the offer clean price is RMB 100.20 per RMB 100 face value, and RMB 20m face value is available. The trader checks the record’s source, time and amounts. The portfolio manager uses the summary to discuss next steps. The approach draws on Southern’s natural-language queries and Aegon-Industrial’s parsing of trading records.

shapes.source: Two information flows across the firm

shapes.name: !!cross.0.0
shapes.english:
Company research
Bond and quote summaries

shapes.name: !!cross.1.1
shapes.english: Review and revise V1 to V2

slides.notes: The first information flow follows Company A. The front office prepares research and bond and quote summaries, the middle office monitors events and related exposures, and the back office maintains the associated documents. The second follows the quarterly client update. The front office drafts V1 from existing views. The author revises it using review findings, and the reviewer checks V2. The back office explains the differences and updates related documents. The links show information reuse and collaboration across teams.

slides.notes:
Employees provide a business question and relevant material. Applications combine LLMs with the tools required for the task. The LLM interprets questions, reads sources, compares explanations and generates text or code. Tools perform queries, calculations and file operations, and execute programs and tests. Shared documents, knowledge bases and business data retain their access rights, references and versions. Qwen and DeepSeek are possible model services to evaluate against the firm’s actual tasks.

slides.title: Proposed implementation sequence

shapes.name: !!phase.0.outputs
shapes.source: Task examples, source catalog and initial applications
shapes.english: Sample tasks, source inventory and initial applications.

shapes.name: !!phase.1.outputs
shapes.source: Field definitions, query interfaces and file workflows
shapes.english: Data definitions, system query interfaces and document workflows.

shapes.name: !!phase.2.outputs
shapes.source: Business tools, user guides and maintenance ownership
shapes.english: Business tools, user guides and named maintenance owners.

slides.notes: Research, sales, compliance and IT can first assemble task examples and source material for research and client-communication applications. Trading, operations and IT can then connect queries and document processing so that the information prepared by the model can be used in subsequent work. Development support and internal services can follow, with clear ownership for maintenance and source updates. Each phase builds on how employees actually use the preceding applications.

shapes.english: Initial focus: research and client communications

shapes.english:
Time from starting the task
to completing the output

shapes.name: !!evaluation.1.body
shapes.source: Whether teams use the analysis and materials
shapes.english: Whether teams use the analysis and materials

shapes.name: !!evaluation.3.body
shapes.source: Whether employees continue to use the application
shapes.english: Whether employees continue to use the application

slides.notes:
Initial focus: research and client communications. Compare similar tasks before and after application use, tracking elapsed task completion time, use of outputs, rework and repeat usage. Use the findings to identify whether the issue is missing information, an unsuitable model explanation or an awkward query or file-handling step. Continued use and reduced preparation work provide a practical basis for deciding what to improve and extend.
Task completion time is the elapsed time from starting the task to completing the output. Repeat usage means whether employees continue to use the application.
